transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~34m
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lena (Redwood SE), Jared (Atlas ML), Priya (Atlas Product), Michael (Atlas CTO)

Summary: quick sync on prefix/KV caching results. Hit rates lower than expected on user-facing routes, likely due to prompt variability and non-canonical keys. Discussed immediate fixes (canonicalize templates, strip session metadata, move static instructions to system prompt), TTL tuning, and potential routing of high-reuse routes to dedicated instances. Agreed next steps and owners.

Transcript:
00:00 Samir: all right thanks everyone for joining, um this is our weekly caching sync. we've got the latest run results from jared so jared do you wanna kick off with what you saw in the 48 hour run?
00:14 Jared: yeah thanks. so we ran the kv - um k v cache profiling over the last two days, it was about, like, 1.2 million requests, average payload like 1.1k tokens i think. overall effective hit rate across all routes was uh about 12 percent which is, yeah lower than we'd hoped. some routes are high, search-qa is around 48% but the user-chat route is like 4 to 6%.
00:36 Lena: okay interesting, do you have breakdown by prompt template? like are the low ones the ones with lots of dynamic fields?
00:44 Jared: exactly, the chat route has a lot of user-specific context, email addresses, timestamps we weren't normalizing, and also there's a ton of slight wording differences - greeting variations, punctuation. also we found the cache keys included session ids in some cases because of how our wrapper builds the request.
00:59 Priya: sorry can i clarify, when you say cache keys included session ids, is that from our front-end or from the middleware?
01:06 Jared: it's mostly our middleware, the wrapper that builds the prompt concatenates a session token for debugging and we didn't strip it before hashing. so every session looked unique.
01:14 Samir: okay that explains a lot. typical pattern. lena, quick thought — canonicalization rules plus moving static instructions into the system prompt should raise reuse. also consider normalized placeholders for user names, dates, and amounts.
01:27 Lena: yeah and on the runtime side we saw that tokenizer differences also caused key mismatches. some of the more subtle punctuation changes change tokenization and the kv prefix isn't matching. we recommend key generation be done on the pretokenized prompt or apply a stable normalization (lowercase, strip punctuation in certain slots).
01:45 Michael: that's interesting, are we able to control that on our end? our stack is node express -> internal wrapper.
01:52 Lena: yes small changes in the wrapper should do it. i'll share example code. basically we do: remove session id, replace dynamic fields with placeholders, move the system-level instructions out of the concatenated prompt and into the model call system prompt. then hash the resulting canonical string.
02:09 Priya: are there any downsides to stripping punctuation? like will it affect model quality?
02:15 Lena: good q — depends. for many intents punctuation doesn't change the meaning. but for some creative generation it can. our suggested approach is route-specific: for transactional/chat support routes you can be aggressive; for NLG-type routes we keep a looser canonicalization. also consider TTL tuning so you don't over-cache ephemeral content.
02:34 Jared: to add, we saw one oddity: some of our front-end sanitizers replace em dashes with hyphens differently across clients, so two otherwise identical prompts ended up different tokens. so normalizing unicode and whitespace helped bump hits by a few points.
02:46 Samir: nice. can you give us numbers after you applied the normalization?
02:50 Jared: yeah quick A/B: baseline chat route 4.3% hit, after stripping session ids + lowercase + placeholdering we got to 18.6% on the sample window, latency p50 dropped ~30ms on cached hits versus misses.
03:05 Samir: that's a solid improvement. so runbook: canonicalize keys, normalize unicode/whitespace, and tune TTLs. on TTL, what are you using now?
03:13 Jared: default was 6 hours for most routes, we tried 24h for one route and saw marginally higher hit rate but also stale responses for some flows — mainly where user context changes fast.
03:23 Lena: TTL should be route and intent specific. also you can add a short-term LRU in the application layer for super-hot prefixes and shorter ttl in kv store. Redwood's runtime supports prefix caching so you can get partial prefix hits even if KV doesn't have a full response.
03:39 Michael: can you explain prefix caching again? i thought kv either hits or misses.
03:44 Lena: sure — prefix caching stores the KV state (like key-value of previous key-steps) so if a later request shares an initial prompt prefix we can reuse the KV cache and only generate subsequent tokens. it's especially effective when users reuse a lot of the same system/instruction text. but it requires stable prefix alignment — small differences break the prefix match.
04:03 Priya: hmm that means our variety in greetings is breaking prefix alignment. do you recommend we canonicalize greetings server-side?
04:10 Lena: yes replace greetings with a placeholder like <GREETING>. also, for dates and amounts replace with <DATE> <AMOUNT>. simple pattern matching works for many cases.
04:18 Jared: one more practical: our hashing used full json of the entire request; switching to canonical string + sha256 dropped collisions and improved reproducibility.
04:26 Samir: ok great. on operational side, two other levers — route skewing to dedicated instance and batching. for routes with very high reuse we can pin them to dedicated capacity to get lower p99 and more consistent kv behavior. are any of the routes high-volume enough to consider that?
04:40 Jared: the support-bot route is ~40k qps per day, not crazy but consistent. could be a candidate.
04:46 Samir: we can model price vs benefit. we'll propose a quick cost/latency tradeoff if you want.
04:51 Priya: yes please. also security check — we need to ensure pii isn't cached. we have to avoid storing PHI/PII in KV. how do we handle that?
04:59 Lena: good point — you can mark keys non-cacheable by route or by using a redaction step before hashing. our recommendation: run a pre-hash redactor to remove email/ssn/cc numbers and either replace with placeholders or flag as non-cacheable. we can share our redaction checklist.
05:16 Michael: and audit logs? we need to show data retention and who accessed caches for compliance.
05:21 Samir: Redwood logs can show per-request cache events and we integrate with your SIEM, and audit trails are available in Dedicated/Private plans. i'll attach SOC2 and retention docs with the priicing addendum.
05:33 Jared: back to metrics — can we track hit rate per-canonical-prefix and have top-n cold keys? that would help identify the noise sources.
05:41 Lena: yes recommend exporting top-100 prefixes by request volume and top-100 misses — send that and we can help pattern-match.
05:48 Samir: next, hashing collisions — we noticed a tiny percent of mismatches, could be due to nondeterministic serialization. ensure stable key ordering.
05:57 Jared: yep we fixed one bug where maps were serialized in iteration order, that removed a source of uniqueness.
06:03 Priya: any automated tooling from Redwood to help with canonicalization?
06:07 Lena: we'll provide starter libraries (python/node) and a small linter that flags suspicious dynamic tokens. not fully automatic but reduces manual work. we'll also include example config for route-specific rules.
06:18 Samir: timeline wise, lena will share code by friday (2026-05-14). jared will run the 24h canonicalized run and share the CSV by tuesday (2026-05-19). samir will send pilot pricing and SOC2 docs by saturday (2026-05-15).
06:33 Michael: sounds good. one more question on model variants — if we fallback to smaller quantized models to save cost will cache behavior change?
06:40 Lena: it can. different model variants sometimes have different tokenization or small generation differences that affect prefix alignment. preferred approach is to pin key routes to a single model family or ensure canonicalization is applied consistently across variants. also consider per-model key namespace if you do routing.
06:58 Priya: ok noted. anything else on experimentation?
07:02 Jared: we'll also try aggressive TTL + client-side validation — if a cached response exists but client signals the context changed, bypass. this hybrid approach helped in other pilots.
07:12 Samir: cool. let's recap next steps — share code, run experiments, share metrics, cost modeling and follow-up benchmark with potential dedicated instance. any objections?
07:22 Michael: none. thanks everyone.
07:25 Samir: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with artifacts and schedule next check-in same time next week unless we need earlier.
07:32 Priya: thanks. bye.

Notes & Links: [Redwood canonicalization examples] (link shared in chat), [SOC2 + Security Addendum] (link), attached sample csv of initial run (uploaded to shared drive).

End of transcript.
